lessons.title: async Function Declarations & Implicit Promises
lessons.description: The async keyword makes a function always return a Promise — even if you return a plain value.

sections.heading: What async does
paragraphs: The async keyword before a function declaration does two things: it lets you use await inside, and it automatically wraps the return value in a Promise.
list: An async function always returns a Promise
If you return a plain value, it's wrapped in Promise.resolve()
If you throw an error, it becomes a rejected Promise
async/await makes async code look and behave like synchronous code

codeExamples.heading: async function basics
explanation: async makes the function always return a Promise.
Returning 42 is the same as returning Promise.resolve(42).
Throwing an error creates a rejected Promise.
This lets you use await to wait for other Promises inside.

practice.task: Write an async function that returns a string. Verify it returns a Promise using .then().

keyTakeaways: The async keyword makes a function return a Promise automatically.
Plain return values are wrapped in Promise.resolve().
async functions enable the use of await inside them.
lessons.challenge: Write an async function that conditionally returns a value or throws an error based on an input parameter. Handle both outcomes.

lessons.title: Pausing Execution with the await Operator
lessons.description: await pauses the async function until a Promise settles — making async code read like synchronous code.

sections.heading: How await works
paragraphs: The await keyword pauses the async function until the Promise resolves, then returns the resolved value. If the Promise rejects, it throws an error.
list: await promise — pauses until the Promise resolves
Returns the resolved value — no .then() needed
If the Promise rejects, it throws — use try/catch
Only works inside async functions (or at the top level in modules)

codeExamples.heading: await in action
explanation: await fetchUser(1) pauses until the Promise resolves.
The resolved value (the user object) is assigned directly to user.
The code reads top-to-bottom like synchronous code.
This is dramatically cleaner than .then() chaining.

practice.task: Write an async function that awaits two sequential delays (1 second each) and logs "Step 1" and "Step 2" between them.
hints: Create a delay(ms) function that returns a Promise.
Total time should be about 2 seconds.

keyTakeaways: await pauses the async function until the Promise settles.
It returns the resolved value or throws on rejection.
Use try/catch around await for error handling.
await makes async code read like synchronous code — a huge readability win.
lessons.challenge: Refactor a .then() chain to use async/await. Compare the readability of both approaches.

lessons.title: Structured Error Handling with try...catch...finally Blocks
lessons.description: Handle async errors cleanly with try/catch — the same pattern you use for synchronous code.

sections.heading: try/catch with async/await
paragraphs: When an awaited Promise rejects, it throws an error. Wrap await calls in try/catch to handle errors gracefully — just like synchronous code.
list: try — contains the code that might throw
catch (error) — handles the error if one occurs
finally — runs regardless of success or failure
Multiple awaits in try — the first error jumps to catch

codeExamples.heading: try/catch with async/await
explanation: try/catch wraps await calls just like it wraps synchronous code.
The catch block receives any error from awaited Promises.
finally runs whether the operation succeeded or failed.
For parallel operations, wrap Promise.all in try/catch.

practice.task: Write an async function that fetches from a URL with try/catch. Simulate both success and failure scenarios.
hints: Use try { let data = await fetch(url); ... } catch (e) { ... }.
Simulate failure by fetching from an invalid URL.
Log different messages for success and error cases.

keyTakeaways: try/catch handles errors from awaited Promises — the same pattern as synchronous code.
catch receives the error object with a message and stack trace.
finally runs regardless of success or failure — great for cleanup.
Wrap Promise.all in try/catch to handle parallel operation failures.
lessons.challenge: Build a data fetching function with retry logic: try 3 times, log each attempt, and only throw if all attempts fail.

lessons.title: Top-Level await in Modern ES Modules
lessons.description: Use await directly at the top level of a module — no need to wrap in an async function.

sections.heading: Top-level await
paragraphs: In ES modules (files with type="module"), you can use await at the top level without wrapping it in an async function.
list: Only works in ES modules (<script type="module"> or .mjs files)
The module execution pauses until the awaited Promise resolves
Other modules that import this one will also wait
Still use try/catch for error handling

codeExamples.heading: Top-level await
explanation: Top-level await works only in ES modules.
The module pauses execution until the Promise resolves.
Importing modules wait for the imported module to finish its top-level await.
This simplifies module initialization that requires async data.

practice.task: Create an HTML file with type="module" script that uses top-level await to fetch data and display it.
hints: In app.js: let data = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).

keyTakeaways: Top-level await lets you use await directly in ES modules.
It pauses the module's execution until the Promise resolves.
Other modules that depend on it will also wait.
Use try/catch for error handling — the same pattern as inside async functions.
lessons.challenge: Create a module that loads configuration from a JSON file using top-level await and exports processed data.
